examples.en-GB: Answer: Creator | Distractors: Judge; Saviour; Lawgiver

data.sourceWord: Covenant with Abraham — promise of descendants and land
data.targetWord: God promised Abraham descendants as numerous as the stars and the land of Canaan. Abraham is considered the father of the Jewish people; the covenant was sealed through circumcision.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 — beliefs about the Covenant with Abraham

data.sourceWord: Covenant with Abraham — blessing to all nations
data.targetWord: God promised that through Abraham all the nations of the earth would be blessed. Jews believe they carry a responsibility as God's Chosen People to be a light to the nations.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 — beliefs about the Covenant with Abraham

data.sourceWord: Abraham influences Jews — monotheism and trust in God
data.targetWord: Belief in Abraham's unwavering trust in one God influences Jews to maintain monotheism, even when it is costly. His willingness to sacrifice his son demonstrates the depth of commitment God expects.

data.sourceWord: Abraham influences Jews — circumcision and Promised Land
data.targetWord: The covenant requirement of circumcision continues to be performed on Jewish baby boys as a sign of belonging to God's covenant community. The Promised Land influences Jews to regard Israel as their homeland.

data.sourceWord: Shekhinah — God's presence in community and worship
data.targetWord: The Shekhinah (divine presence) rests among Jews when ten are gathered in prayer. It is felt at the Western Wall and during communal Torah study, showing God's continued closeness to his people.
The Shekhinah was manifested as a pillar of fire and cloud during the Exodus, and was present in Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem. Some Reform Jews see it as the feminine presence of God.

data.sourceWord: Scripture: Moses and God face to face
data.targetWord: 'And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face.' (Deuteronomy 34:10) — showing the unique relationship Moses had with God.

data.sourceWord: FOR: All 613 mitzvot are commanded by God
data.targetWord: God commands Jews to follow all 613 mitzvot. The Torah states they are equally sacred and binding, and the story of Adam and Eve shows the consequences of disobeying even one divine command.

data.sourceWord: FOR: Mitzvot cover all aspects of Jewish life
data.targetWord: The mitzvot instruct Jews on worship, ethical behaviour, diet, business and community life — providing a complete framework for living as God's people in every situation.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Free will allows Jews to prioritise mitzvot
data.targetWord: 'Everything is foreseen, yet free will is granted.' (Pirkei Avot) — Jews have free will and may choose which mitzvot to prioritise, especially when a life is at risk (Pikuach Nefesh allows breaking commandments to save life).

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Many mitzvot are ancient and difficult to apply today
data.targetWord: Many of the 613 mitzvot relate to Temple worship or agricultural contexts no longer relevant. Progressive Jews argue the Torah must be interpreted for each generation rather than followed literally.

data.answer: God promised Abraham descendants and the land of Canaan.
The Shekhinah is the divine presence of God among his people.

data.prompt: What is the sign of the covenant with Abraham?
data.answer: Circumcision is the sign of the covenant with Abraham.

data.title: The Torah and the Covenant at Sinai
data.sourceTitle: The Torah and the Covenant at Sinai
data.sourcePassage: The Torah is the most sacred text in Judaism, containing the first five books of the Hebrew Bible (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy). At its heart is the covenant God made with the Jewish people at Mount Sinai through Moses. God gave the Jewish people the Ten Commandments and the 613 mitzvot (commandments) as the terms of the covenant — instructions for how to live as God's holy people. In return, God promised to be their God and to protect and bless them. The Torah scroll is the most sacred object in the synagogue, kept in the Ark and read publicly each week. Orthodox Jews believe the Torah is the literal word of God, written by Moses under divine inspiration, and that all 613 mitzvot must be followed. Conservative and Reform Jews take a more flexible view, believing the Torah is divinely inspired but written by humans, and that some commandments can be adapted for modern life. Despite these differences, all Jewish denominations agree that the Torah is central to Jewish identity and practice.
